title: Content with what comes
hookLine: contentment isn't getting what you want but wanting what comes (Discourses 1.12)

lines: SPELLING YOUR NAME YOUR OWN WAY.
cards: A child learning to write her name sometimes wants to spell it her own way: an extra letter here, a backward one there, because she likes how it looks. The teacher gently says no: your name is spelled like this.

And at some point the child stops fighting it, and starts wanting to write it the way it really is. Epictetus suspected plenty of adults are still at the stage of the backward letter, with their whole lives.

teach.h: WHAT PEOPLE BELIEVE ABOUT THE GODS.
teach.b: Discourses book one, chapter twelve, is on contentment. Epictetus starts with a survey of what people believe about the gods. Some say there are none.
Some say they exist but do nothing. Some say they care for the heavens but not for us. Some say they care for us, but only in general.
And some, like Socrates, say they're aware of every move we make. He sides with the last, and builds on it.

If the world is ordered by reason, then being educated, he says, means learning to want things to happen as they actually do happen. That's the radical line: not getting what you want, but wanting what comes.
When I learn to write a name, he says, I don't get to spell it however I like. I learn to want it the way it is. Same with music.
Same, he says, with life. Isn't that just giving up? Epictetus says no, with a surprising example.
Socrates sat in prison, but he wasn't imprisoned, because he was there willingly.
A prison, for Epictetus, is a place you're held against your will. Take away the against, and the walls are just walls.
Not everyone accepts the Stoic picture of a reasoning universe behind events, and Epictetus himself lists those who don't.
But his practice can be tried by anyone: stop fighting the spelling of the day, and see what changes.

how: Some Stoic practitioners take one unchosen event of the day, a delay or a disappointment, and rehearse wanting it as it is rather than as they wished it to be.

o: the man in prison who wasn't imprisoned, being there willingly
the teacher who escaped prison with his friends' help
the student who wrote down Epictetus' lessons

games.q: content with what comes: tap the pairs.
p: spell it the way it is
a place held against your will

s: Epictetus says contentment means getting what you want
he says it means wanting what actually happens.
chapter 1.12 opens with a survey of what people believe about the gods
from those who say there are none to those, like Socrates, who say the gods see every move.
Epictetus says Socrates in prison wasn't truly imprisoned
he was there willingly, and a prison is where you're held against your will.

games.q: you're learning to write a name, and you'd like to spell it your own way. what does Epictetus say an educated person does?
o: learns to want it the way it really is.
refuses to write it at all.
games.why: he uses writing and music to show that education is learning to want things as they are, and then applies it to life.

practice: Think of one thing that came today that you didn't choose, the weather, a delay, a mood in the house, an ache, and notice the small push against it. For a few breaths, try to want it as it is: not to like it, just to stop pushing.
If the push comes back, that's fine; notice it, and let it go again.

wordCard.voice: Socrates, who sat in prison but wasn't imprisoned, because he was there willingly: Epictetus' picture of wanting things as they actually happen. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: content. Not liking everything, just no longer fighting the spelling. Day three hundred ninety-eight.
